blocks.text: Regardless of electrophile used, the electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism can be divided into three main steps.

items: Generation of electrophile: The first step of an electrophilic substitution reaction involves the generation of an electrophile. The electrophile can be a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule. Typically, electrophiles cannot simply be added to the reaction mixture. The electrophile is produced in situ, by adding appropriate reagents to the reaction mixture.

Electrophilic attack: In the second step the π electrons of benzene attack the electrophile. This forms a sigma bond between one carbon atom of the benzene ring and the electrophile. This disrupts the aromaticity in the ring as there are now only four π electrons and there is a positive charge spread over the five carbon atoms. Because of the new sigma bond formed, this intermediate is called a sigma complex.

Restoration of aromaticity: In the 3rd step, the hydrogen on the sp³-hybridized carbon is removed by a counterion/conjugate base restoring the aromaticity to the ring. This happens by heterolytic cleavage of the C-H bond. This means that the electrons in this bond go into the benzene π bonding system, and the d-localisation in the ring is restored

blocks.alt: Benzene with a curly arrow from its ring to E+, then the sigma complex: a ring whose top carbon carries H and E, with a broken circle and a + inside and a curly arrow from the C-H bond into the ring. A second arrow labelled Rapid step gives the substituted benzene with E, + H+.
blocks.caption: General mechanism of electrophilic substitution (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 65).

blocks.text: Examples of electrophilic substitution reactions of arenes are given as follows.
Halogenation of Benzene
Benzene only reacts with bromine and chlorine in the presence of Lewis acids as they coordinate to the halogens and generate strong electrophilic species.
The Lewis acids are usually aluminum chloride (AlCl₃), iron chloride (FeCl₃) or iron bromide (FeBr₃).
This is bromination of benzene, which involves following steps:

blocks.alt: Benzene + Br2, with AlBr3 over the arrow and ANHYDROUS under it, gives bromobenzene + HBr.
blocks.caption: Bromination of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 65).

blocks.alt: Br-Br with delta+ on the left bromine and delta- on the right one; a curly arrow goes from the delta- bromine to AlBr3. The arrow gives Br+ + [AlBr4]-.
blocks.caption: Formation of the electrophile Br+ from Br2 and AlBr3 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 65).

blocks.text: Once the electrophile is formed, it follows the same general mechanism as we have discussed earlier.

blocks.alt: Benzene with a green curly arrow from the ring to Br+, giving the sigma complex with Br and H on one carbon and + in the broken ring. [AlBr4]- sends a curly arrow to that H and a curly arrow runs from the C-H bond into the ring. The arrow gives bromobenzene + HBr + AlBr3.
blocks.caption: Attack of Br+ and loss of the proton in the bromination of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 65-66).

blocks.text: First, the addition of the electrophile, forming the sigma complex which is then deprotonated by AlCl₄⁻

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed scheme marks the partial charges on Br–Br as σ+ and σ−; partial charges are δ+ and δ−, as drawn above. The regenerated catalyst printed “[AlBr₃)” is AlBr₃. In bromination the sigma complex is deprotonated by [AlBr₄]⁻, not AlCl₄⁻ as the text says.
In the same way, FeCl₃ is used as the Lewis acid activator for generating Cl⁺. The rest of the mechanism is identical to what we saw for the bromination of benzene.

blocks.title: Quick Check 20.4
blocks.text: a) Write mechanism of reaction of benzene with chlorine using AlCl₃ as catalyst.
Nitration of Benzene
Nitro group is introduced on benzene, using mixture of conc. HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄. The mechanism involves the following steps:

blocks.alt: Benzene + HNO3, with H2SO4 over the arrow, gives nitrobenzene + H2O.
blocks.caption: Nitration of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 66).

items: The electrophile NO₂⁺ ion is generated by reacting concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃) and concentrated sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄).
A pair of electrons from the benzene ring is donated to the NO₂⁺ electrophile to form a covalent bond causing a loss in aromaticity
The C–H bond of the substituted carbon atom breaks and the electrons go back into the benzene π bonding system, restoring its aromaticity

blocks.text: Mechanism

blocks.alt: Three steps. Formation of Electrophile: H2SO4 + HNO3 in equilibrium with NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O, with NO2+ tagged electrophile. Attack of Electrophile: a curly arrow from the benzene ring to NO2+ gives the sigma complex with H and NO2 on one carbon; a curly arrow from the C-H bond into the ring gives nitrobenzene + H+. Regeneration of the Catalyst: HSO4- + H+ gives H2SO4, tagged catalyst.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the nitration of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 66).

blocks.text: Concentrated sulphuric acid acts as a catalyst so is not written in the equations. At higher temperatures there is a greater chance of getting more than one nitro group substituted onto the ring. You will get a certain amount of 1,3-dinitrobenzene formed even at 50°C.

blocks.alt: Nitrobenzene + HNO3, with 50 degrees C over the arrow, gives 1,3-dinitrobenzene + H2O.
blocks.caption: Formation of 1,3-dinitrobenzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 67).

Friedel-Crafts Alkylation and Acylation

In the Friedel-Crafts acylation reaction, an acyl group is substituted into the benzene ring in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst. An acyl group is an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group, R-C=O. In the Friedel-Crafts alkylation, an alkyl group is substituted into the benzene ring.

blocks.alt: Friedel-Crafts Alkylation: benzene + CH3CH2Cl, heat over the arrow and AlCl3 catalyst under it, gives ethylbenzene + HCl. Friedel-Crafts Acylation: benzene + CH3CH2COCl, heat and AlCl3 catalyst, gives the ring carrying C(=O)CH2CH3 + HCl.
blocks.caption: Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 67).

blocks.text: a) Friedel-Crafts Alkylation
The Friedel-Crafts alkylation reaction proceeds via a three-step mechanism.

items: The Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl₃) undergoes reaction with the alkyl halide, resulting in the formation of a carbocation which acts as an electrophile.

blocks.alt: (CH3)3C-Cl, the Lewis base, with lone pairs on Cl, + AlCl3, the Lewis acid; a curly arrow goes from a Cl lone pair to AlCl3. This gives Cl(+)-AlCl3(-) still bonded to the carbon, with a curly arrow from the C-Cl bond to Cl. The products are the 3 degree carbocation (CH3)3C+, labelled electrophile - E+, and [Cl-AlCl3]-.
blocks.caption: Formation of the carbocation in Friedel-Crafts alkylation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 67).

items: The π electrons of aromatic ring attack on electrophilic carbocation, forming an arenium ion as an intermediate. The aromaticity of the arene is temporarily lost due to the breakage of the carbon-carbon double bond.

The deprotonation of the intermediate leads to the reformation of the carbon-carbon double bond, restoring aromaticity to the compound. This proton goes on to form hydrochloric acid, regenerating the AlCl₃ catalyst.

blocks.alt: Forming a new carbon-carbon bond: a curly arrow from benzene to the tertiary carbocation (addition of the electrophile) gives a resonance structure of the sigma complex, the ring carbon carrying H and C(CH3)3 and a + in the ring. Loss of a proton, restoring the aromaticity: [Cl-AlCl3]- sends a curly arrow to the H and a curly arrow runs from the C-H bond into the ring; with -AlCl3 under the arrow this gives tert-butylbenzene + HCl.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of Friedel-Crafts alkylation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 68).

blocks.text: b) Friedel-Crafts Acylation
Friedel-Crafts acylations proceed through a four-step mechanism.

items: A reaction occurs between the Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl₃) and the acyl halide. A complex is formed and the acyl halide loses a halide ion, forming an acylium ion.

blocks.alt: R-C(=O)-Cl, the Lewis base, with lone pairs on Cl, + AlCl3, the Lewis acid, gives the complex R-C(=O)-Cl(+)-AlCl3(-), which gives the acylium ion R-C(+)=O and [Cl-AlCl3]-.
blocks.caption: Formation of the acylium ion in Friedel-Crafts acylation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 68).

items: An electrophilic attack of π electrons of the aromatic ring on the acylium ion (RCO⁺) takes place.

The intermediate complex is now deprotonated, restoring the aromaticity to the ring. This proton attaches itself to a chloride ion, forming HCl. The AlCl₃ catalyst is regenerated. Thus, the required acyl benzene product is obtained via the Friedel-Crafts acylation reaction.

blocks.alt: A curly arrow from benzene to the carbon of R-C(+)=O, whose O carries a lone pair and a curly arrow from the C=O bond to O, gives a resonance structure of the sigma complex with H and C(=O)R on one ring carbon and + in the ring. [Cl-AlCl3]- sends a curly arrow to the H, and a curly arrow runs from the C-H bond into the ring; with -AlCl3 under the arrow this gives the aryl ketone, the ring carrying C(=O)R.
blocks.caption: Mechanism of Friedel-Crafts acylation (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 68).

blocks.text:
1. Write down reactions of methyl benzene with bromine in the presence of AlBr₃.
2. Explain the difference in the reactivity of bromine with benzene and with phenol. Include the type of reaction, the products that form, and any conditions required. Mechanisms for the reactions are not required.
3. Explain the difference in the reactivity of bromine with benzene and with ethyl benzene. Include the type of reaction, the products that form, and any conditions required. Mechanisms for the reactions are not required.
4. Which of 1,1-dimethyethyllbenzene and methyl benzene is easier to form by Friedel-Craft reaction? Explain based on the stability of carbocation.
